article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: London-based Capture has declared that Joe Swanberg ’s romantic drama The Sun Never Sets , starring Dakota Fanning , Jake Johnson and Cory Michael Smith, is sold-out as it unveils a raft of international deals.

The picture the film has sold to Italy (Minerva), Scandinavia (NonStop) Portugal (NOS), Turkey (Chantier), former Yugoslavia (Jucer), Middle East (Phoenicia), Latin America (Synapse) and international airlines (Cinesky).

Focus Features has acquired the rest of the world (excluding Italy, Scandinavia, Portugal, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and Latin America) with Universal Pictures International set to handle international distribution for the studio.

Related Stories

Focus Features & Blumhouse-Atomic Monster Snap Up Micro-Budget Horror Film 'Play House' From Nicolas Curcio

Shot on 35mm against the backdrop of Anchorage, Alaska, the film had its world premiere at the 2026 SXSW Film Festival. It was released theatrically in the U.S. by IFC Films and in Canada by Mongrel Media.

Watch on Deadline

Written and directed by Swanberg ( Drinking Buddies, Happy Christmas ), The Sun Never Sets stars Fanning as a free-spirited woman whose seemingly happy relationship with an older, divorced father (Johnson) is thrown into question when he suggests they take a break.

When she then unexpectedly reconnects with her former boyfriend Chuck), a complicated love triangle develops forcing her to confront what she really wants from life and love.

The ensemble cast also includes Debby Ryan, Anna Konkle, Lamorne Morris and Karley Sciortino.

“ The Sun Never Sets has been a joy to represent, and the response from international buyers has been fantastic. We’re thrilled to have secured such a strong roster of distribution partners, including Focus Features across multiple territories, bringing a hugely successful international sales campaign to a close,” said Ella Field, EVP of International Sales at Capture.

The film is produced by Swanberg, Fanning, Johnson, Smith and Ashleigh Snead.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Director Jason Perlman’s Bad Influence has rounded out the cast of the YA horror film, which has recently wrapped filming.

Joining the ensemble, which includes previously announced stars Xochitl Gomez, Madeleine McGraw and Jack Champion, are John Cho ( Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , Harold & Kumar ), Ethan Suplee ( Twisted Metal , My Name Is Earl ), Danny Jolles ( Hacks , Crazy Ex-Girlfriend ), Arnas Fedaravičius ( The White Lotus ), Ana Ortiz ( Imperfect Women , Ugly Betty ), Jacob Vargas ( Sons of Anarchy , National Treasure: Edge of History ) and Michelle Macedo ( High Potential ).

From screenwriter Brandon Cohen, Bad Influence is described as a modern-day Thelma & Louise fueled by female rage, following Isabelle (McGraw) and Kira (Gomez) on a road trip home for spring break, when they pick up mysterious hitchhiker (Liam), who is not what he seems.

Watch on Deadline

Xochitl Gomez, Madeleine McGraw & Jack Champion Cast In ‘Bad Influence’ YA Horror

Kal Penn’s Busy Onscreen Year Includes Playing Anna Nicole Smith’s Doctor, A Gregg Araki Role & ‘Harold & Kumar 4’ In Works: “One Of The Funniest Scripts”

Bad Influence producers are Debbie Liebling, Joel David Moore and Zachary Burgess. Moore and Liebling previously collaborated on Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story (2004) and Grandma’s Boy (2006). Executive producers include Steven Silverstein, Cathy Raduns, Raymond Merrill, Carmelo Chimera, Syed Ali Saeed, Denis Schoenhofer, Natalie Kline, Jarod Einsohn and Michelle and Melissa Macedo.

Cho is repped by UTA, 3 Arts and Yorn Levine; Suplee by Paradigm, Nicole Garcia Management and Hansen Jacobson; Jolles by Innovative Artists, Framework Entertainment, and Knol Hanly Garrett; Fedaravičius by The Artists Partnership and Link Entertainment; and Ortiz by Gersh Agency.

Capture is handling sales on Bad Influence .

article_text:
Paul McCartney has a bone to pick with Sam Mendes , the director of the upcoming four Beatles movies starring Paul Mescal as McCartney, Harris Dickinson as John Lennon, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison and Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr. What’s the issue? It all comes down to how tall Mescal is compared to his co-stars.

“We were all the same height!” McCartney declared on the “Good Hang” podcast, noting how movies based on the Beatles wrongly depict him as shorter than his bandmates. “We were all the same height, and Ringo was a bit smaller. And if you look at photos, we’re all the same height.”

Related Stories

Marjoe Gortner, Preacher and Actor Who Was Subject of Oscar-Winning Doc and Appeared in 'Earthquake,' 'Falcon Crest,' Dies at 82

Mark Mortimer, 'Another World' Soap Opera Star, Dies at 59

“Guess what?” McCartney added about Mescal. “He is smaller than the guy who plays John. Sam Mendes is making the film. I said, ‘Sam, I’ve got just one thing that I need to say to you. You know, Paul [Mescal is] a bit smaller.’ I don’t know how Sam’s gonna deal with it. He sent me a picture, a still from the filming they were doing, and they’re crossing the Abbey Road crossing, and the Paul character is markedly smaller. I texted him: ‘Sam! Smaller? Don’t do this! You said you wouldn’t do it.’”

Popular on Variety

McCartney also once expressed his frustration to Sam Taylor-Johnson, director of 2009’s “Nowhere Boy,” which starred Aaron Taylor-Johnson as a teenage John Lennon. Thomas Brodie-Sangster had a supporting role as McCartney in the biographical drama but is shorter than Taylor-Johnson.

“The John character, who she later married, Aaron — he’s bigger than me in the film,” McCartney said. “My character is kind of wimpy. Smaller than John. John knocks me to the floor. And it’s like, ‘Sam, this is not true!’ Her only explanation, bless her, because she’s still a good friend, she said, ‘This is a movie, it’s not a documentary.’ And I thought, ‘Well, I don’t like that explanation.’ But I couldn’t do anything, because by now she’d made the film. There was I, little Paul. John, the great big hero, and it’s like: No! It’s not true.”

Mendes is directing four Beatles movies, one centered on each of the band members. The project, officially titled “The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event,” has the backing of Sony Pictures and is currently in the middle of its year-long production. All four movies will be released theatrically in April 2028.

“We want people to be able to experience them in the cinema at the same during the same period,” producer Pippa Harris recently said at the BFI London Film Festival , noting she does not expect audiences to “see all four films on the same day.”

“Within the same month — you might see one a week, or you might see one weekend and two the next and one the next. However you see it, I think our hope is that people will see all four films,” she added.

Watch McCartney’s full interview on “Good Hang” in the video below.

article_text:
Born in London in 1965, Keith Brymer Jones is a potter, ceramic designer and TV judge. After a stint as lead singer of the punk band the Wigs, he became an apprentice at Harefield Pottery in London. He went on to set up his own company, and created pots and homewares for retailers including Conran, Habitat and Laura Ashley, before developing his signature Word range . He has been a judge on The Great Pottery Throw Down since it started in 2015. His new book, Firing Earth: An Unexpected History of Pots and Potters, is published on 22 October.

This photo was taken in our family home in Finchley. Socks, shorts and a T-shirt was my usual outfit for scabbing around in the garden aged 11. I was a complete and utter square.

My main passion at this time was dancing – ballet, tap and Highland and Scottish country dancing. But I was starting to realise I should stop telling people about it. I was about to embark on my first year of secondary school at St Mary’s in Hendon and knew I’d get stick for it.

I kept it under wraps, but I was bullied for three years. It was the start of a difficult part of my life, especially after my grandfather died. His death happened in front of me, when he fell down the stairs while having a heart attack. Unsurprisingly, my OCD developed around this time; I used it to try to create a sense of control and order. Everything around me had to be at 90 degrees – pens, pencils and the curtains. My bedroom began to resemble an empty studio, because it was easier than having belongings. To this day, I do like a tidy workshop.

Although starting secondary school was traumatic, 11 was also the age I discovered clay. Back in the 80s, if you had dyslexia, you were considered thick, but as soon as I started to manipulate this material into shape, form and volume, I understood it. It felt like a religious calling – an epiphany – and it was the first time any teacher said I was good at something.

Very quickly, creativity became an obsession . I would stay in the art room during the lunch break and before and after school. Some of the bullies found out and put razor blades in the clay. I’d be throwing on the wheel and all of a sudden I’d feel a nick in the clay. At first I’d think it was a stone, but I’d look down and my hands were covered in cuts. Soon after that the teachers locked the door and gave me a key. By the time I was in sixth form, I would bunk off school to go to the V&A museum and spend the whole day looking at pots.

I grew up in a typical household for the time: my father went to work and my mother was a stay-at-home mum. She was a cookery teacher before they got married, and my sister and I would come home from school to find a piece of cake and a pint of milk waiting for us. Dad had a well-paid job as a head of a building society, but he hated it. Sport was his big thing. He once said to me in the car: “Whatever you do, Keith, make sure you do a job that you really love because you’ll be doing it for 85% of your life.” My sister was a high-achieving academic student, so my parents were a bit worried about where I might end up.

Much to their relief, shortly after I finished school I started my career as a clayboy at Harefield. I was a grafter, and by the end of my eight years there, I was head of production. This was also when I started to look like a bricklayer, because I used to have to shovel 10 tonnes of clay every two weeks. I was eating two lunches a day and five Mars bars just to keep the energy going. The owners were total anarchists who just happened to be potters.

When Harefield moved up to Inverness, I decided to set up my own studio in London. I wanted to make the best of it, and worked relentlessly. My largest ever order was a breakfast range for Habitat – 16,000 pieces that I made by hand. Some evenings I’d be cleaning my hands and I’d see a white mark and wonder what it was, only to realise it was the knuckle bone. It didn’t hurt, because it happened over time and I have a high pain threshold. When I did ballet, my father, who was also really practical, used to take me down to the garage and pull out my big toenails with a pair of pliers because I wanted to get a better point.

My path to ending up on TV happened in an unconventional way. One day Dom, my business partner, phoned up and said: “We should do a video like Adele’s for Rolling in the Deep – she’s in this old mansion and there’s all this broken crockery being smashed. My aunt’s got a mansion – we can do it there.” We rocked up, filmed a parody and the video went viral . It got into the hands of a woman who knew Richard McKerrow, the head honcho of Love Productions at the time, and happened to be looking into a new pottery format. She piped up and said: “Have a look at this cross‑dressing potter who’s done an Adele video.” He saw it and asked if I wanted to be a judge on The Great Pottery Throw Down.

after newsletter promotion

I wasn’t convinced at first, as I know how long it takes to make a pot – 11 days, from start to finish. I was also adamant I didn’t want to make car-crash TV, where you’re just waiting for people to fail. But over a lot of wine, McKerrow convinced me to do it.

I had no idea I was going to be emotional on camera, but within 10 minutes of the first episode, it began. Someone was in trouble in the studio – I really felt for her, and started crying. In my earpiece, I heard one of the directors saying: “Fucking hell, one of the judges is crying. This is TV gold.” I still get a lot of messages from men who are grateful to see me being emotional. Even today I was walking past a building site and some bloke goes: “Oh, it’s that bloke that cries on the telly! Well done, mate!” I very rarely get any negative feedback about crying, because it’s honest.

These days, I have a strong sense of who I am and feel very comfortable in my own skin, but it took a while to get to that place. It all started after my mother died in my 20s. I had just set up my own studio, and because I was grieving and working so hard, I was getting panic attacks. I began bereavement counselling, and it was the first time I realised my emotional state could affect my physical state. Since then, I’ve had quite a bit of therapy and can finally feel confident in who I am. Something that boy, hiding his love of dancing, being a total square, couldn’t conceive of.

Firing Earth by Keith Brymer Jones (Hodder & Stoughton, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

article_text:
In 1962, the then French culture minister, André Malraux, reportedly bored by the ballet he was watching at Paris’s opera house, raised his eyes to the classical ceiling and decided it needed a makeover.

In his ennui, Malraux thought his friend and artist Marc Chagall , sitting next to him at the Palais Garnier at the time, was the man for the job and commissioned him to make a new ceiling.

Over the next two years, Chagall worked in secret and for free to produce 24 enormous and colourful wedge-shaped canvases, that were installed over the original 19th-century classical ceiling by the now forgotten artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu.

Today, more than four decades after Chagall’s death, one of Lenepveu’s descendants is planning legal action to have the original ceiling uncovered and restored.

Arnaud Carayon says he has “asked nicely” for this to happen for three years, including writing two letters to France’s president, Emmanuel Macron. Now he has instructed a lawyer to take the fight to court.

“The Lenepveu ceiling is classified as a historic monument and yet it hasn’t been seen for 60 years and we have no idea what state it is in,” Carayon said.

“Today, everyone has forgotten Lenepveu. Unfortunately, he was swept away by the wave of impressionism, but in his time he was really a star. More importantly, he was specifically chosen to decorate the opera ceiling by Charles Garnier, who designed everything in the opera house right down to the last door knob.

“But on a whim, Malraux decided he did not agree with Garnier’s choice.”

Garnier’s opera house was commissioned by Napoleon III and opened in January 1875 in the presence of European royals and political figures including the then lord mayor of London, Sir William Cotton.

Lenepveu, who was Garnier’s friend and artistic collaborator, produced a classical and allegorical work painted in oil directly on the copper plates of the dome. The work, called The Muses and the Hours of Day and Night, and given historic listing in 1923, was considered perfectly in keeping with the ornate Second Empire style of Garnier’s palace.

Lenepveu, who went on to lead the French Academy in Rome, later produced a series of Joan of Arc frescoes in the Paris Panthéon, but his name is little known today.

Malraux is said to have wanted to give the fusty opera house a more modern, edgy feel. Chagall’s 24 cake-slice shaped canvases were spliced together around the central chandelier covering 220 sq metres (2,368 sq ft) of the dome. The work is divided into separate colours: red, blue, green, yellow and white; and features dancers, angels, musicians and the names of composers.

Even before Chagall’s work was installed, the row between traditionalists and modernists erupted and reached the other side of the Channel.

The Royal Institute of British Architects in London wrote to the culture minister asking him to abandon his plans to cover the original ceiling. “The unique character of this edifice [the opera house] is based on the fact that all its elements: architecture, paintings, sculptures and mosaics work together in harmony,” Riba wrote. Its plea was ignored.

The Palais Garnier will be closed for renovation between 2027-32, and Carayon, the president of the Friends of Lenepveu Society, said he had written to Macron to suggest alternating the Lenepveu and Chagall ceilings after it reopens, with each being shown for a decade. He said the Élysée Palace replied only that the president was “particularly attentive” to the subject.

“From the beginning, the Chagall ceiling was designed to be removable. It can be taken down without any damage. We thought the idea of alternating ceilings was very positive and promising, but it seems nobody has the guts to touch the Chagall ceiling,” Carayon said.

At a 2023-24 Chagall exhibition at the Pompidou Centre, the curator, Anne Montfort-Tanguy, said: “The ceiling [of the opera house] is Chagall: it’s his autobiography, his vision of Paris. All the artists he loved are represented as well as what he considered the most important Paris monuments like the Eiffel Tower … It’s a moving, fluid almost cinematic work. The ceiling is a complete work of art.

“It was Chagall’s gift to the country that welcomed him; an homage to France and to Paris,” Montfort-Tanguy added.

Alexander Neef, the director of the Paris Opera, told Le Monde : “The debate over the Chagall ceiling has gone on for more than 60 years. The Lenepveu ceiling has been listed as a historic monument since 1923 so its heritage value is recognised. That his [Lenepveu’s] descendants wish to defend his memory is legitimate.”

article_text:
Selma Blair ‘s spokesperson has spoken out after the actress was charged with second-degree assault following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday.

“Since Sunday night, the public account of what happened to Selma aboard a flight to New York has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline,” her spokesperson told People .

“A handful of journalists have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline, and we are grateful to them,” the statement continued. “But fair reporting has been the exception, and in the space left by our silence, speculation has hardened into something being treated as fact. We can, however, correct the record on a few points already in public circulation. Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight. There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”

Related Stories

Netflix’s 'Haunted Hotel' Renewed for Season 3

Russell Brand Documentary From 'Jimmy Savile: A British Horror Story' Producers Set at Netflix Days After Rape Sentencing

The spokesperson added, “The suggestion by anyone that Selma does not have multiple sclerosis is outrageous. Her diagnosis has been public since 2018. What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle. She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily. Selma also has pseudobulbar affect, a neurological condition secondary to her MS, which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her. For the same reason, she travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side, and the authorities took her dog from her.”

Blair “has worked on seven film and television projects in 2026 alone, only a couple of which have been announced. She has launched a skin care line, a clothing line, and a line of eye-glass readers, each built around the idea of beauty and utility for people whose bodies do not always cooperate. She remains a visible and relentless advocate for disability rights, for the MS community, and this year for the Jewish community in the face of rising antisemitism, including from the stage of the ADL’s State of the Arts event at The Jewish Museum two weeks ago. Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night. There is much more to this story than has been reported, and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion,” the statement concluded.

Blair was arrested on Sunday, Oct. 11 for an incident that occurred after she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another on a Delta plane heading from Los Angeles to New York. Law enforcement was waiting for the 54-year-old “Legally Blonde” actress at John F. Kennedy airport, where police took her into custody and transported her to a hospital for evaluation. The arrest was due to her allegedly attacking a police officer and a nurse after being removed from the plane. She could also face federal charges for the incident on board the aircraft.

A representative for Blair told Variety : “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

The FBI opened an investigation relating to the incident, as the agency does with all assaults aboard aircraft. A Delta Air Lines spokesperson told Variety , “Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.” Despite the chaos on board, there was no operational impact to the flight, which landed at JFK ahead of schedule at approximately 11 p.m.

On Monday, Variety reported that Blair had received second-degree assault charges after her arrest, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released later that evening.

This incident was not the first time Blair had an outburst on a plane. In 2016, she was removed from a flight on a stretcher while traveling with her 4-year-old son after she “had a total psychotic blackout.” Blair chalked up the incident to drinking a glass of wine and taking a pill, saying at the time, “It was horrible and frightening and I had empathy for myself actually afterwards because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother.”

article_text:
Qatar’s Doha Film Festival has pulled Fing! from its program following sexual misconduct allegations against UK actor and writer David Walliams who wrote the book on which it is based.

The family movie, which world premiered in Sundance, was due to make its international premiere as part of the festival’s gala lineup this Friday.

The decision to remove the film from the program was made within hours o f news breaking on Tuesday that Walliams was at the heart of allegations involving exploitative sexual activity with girls and young women.

Related Stories

BBC Boss Challenged By Staff Over Culture Of "Reverence" Towards Powerful Stars

BBC Boss Matt Brittin & Industry Leaders Set To Attend Culture Secretary's Emergency Meeting Next Week Following Brand & Walliams Scandals

Little Britain star Walliams, who has denied the allegations, had sought to prevent the publication of a joint investigation by the UK’s ITN News and The Guardian newspaper with an injunction. The allegations have sent shock waves through the UK entertainment world and beyond.

Watch on Deadline

Ticketholders for the Fing! gala event in Doha were informed that the screening had been cancelled and that full refunds would be given. The festival has confirmed the decision to Deadline.

It was first announced in October that Fing! would play in the Doha Film Festival as part of its gala program also featuring Paper Tiger , Furies , Edward Said: Between Worlds and Bruno Dumont’s Red Rocks .

Based on Walliams’ eponymous 2019 children’s book, Fing! stars Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska, Matt Lucas and Iona Bell and is directed by Australian director Jeffrey Walker. Walliams co-wrote the screenplay.

It is produced by AGC Studios, Bondit Media Capital in L.A., Elevate Media Production in Australia and Walliams’ production company King Bert.

The producers announced on Tuesday that they had cut Walliams from a cameo scene , while a number of distributors have cancelled or scaled back release plans.

Comcast-owned Sky has pulled out as the UK and Ireland licensee of the film, while in Australia, its distributor Transmission Films has said it will remove Walliams from its publicity campaign, and streamer distributor Stan has said it will no longer release the movie.

As of Tuesday, family friendly-distributor Angel, which acquired Fing! in May, said it was pushing on with a scheduled release in early 2027.

The Doha Film Festival runs from November 19 to 27, 2026.

"主角是马特·哈根（汤姆·里斯·哈里斯饰），一位正在崭露头角的演员，他因偶然与一名黑帮头目交集而导致面部毁容。他所遭受的暴力随着行业因其外貌尽失而迅速抛弃他的现实而愈发恶化。在看不到恢复希望的情况下，他找到了科学家凯特琳·科尔（娜奥米·阿基饰），后者采用纳米细胞的地下治疗手段提供了一种自我修复的可能。然而，这种干预对他的身体产生了两人都无法控制的影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "剧本、导演和剪辑以极快的节奏组织了这段历程。片中有足够的信息来理解这位演员的处境及其选择的紧迫性，既没有过长的旁白铺陈，也没有要求观众具备对DC以往作品的先前了解。每一次试图解决问题的尝试都会引发新的困境，赋予了影片客观性，同时又没有使其流于表面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当剧情开始探索其超能力的种种可能时，哈根的痛苦依然存在，这防止了身体恐怖仅仅沦为一堆令人反感的视觉奇观。这种治疗直接干扰了他试图重回被中断生活的努力，而将一个已经伤痕累累的人置于一种让其身体更难控制的程序中，本身就带着一种残酷的讽刺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "汤姆·里斯·哈里斯是影片运转的核心要素，他的眼神传达出一种脆弱感，即便在他开始做出难以辩护的举动时依然清晰可见。他的表演让观众得以跟随这一转变过程，既没有将哈根简化为逆来顺受的受害者，也没有将他的悲惨遭遇变成其一切行为的自动正当化理由。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "娜奥米·阿基饰演的凯特琳维持着一种超越提供治疗职责的关系。这位科学家对演员的同情赋予了她干预后果以分量，而没有依赖纯粹的浪漫纠葛。她的参与让哈根的痛苦与一个试图帮助他、同时又必须应对自己所造成后果的人紧密相连。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "瓦特金斯巧妙地运用了密闭的空间以及光影之间的对比。光线的局限限制了可视范围，使封闭空间成为一种忧虑的来源，从而避免了威胁完全依赖于展示哈根变形后的身体。在室外，哥谭市并不像在《小丑》中那样具有绝对的主角地位，尽管它高效地暗示了一种衰败，而无需对其地理风貌或神话体系进行过多的铺垫。这座城市服务于故事的氛围，正如喜剧调剂的匮乏使得不适感得以不间断地延续一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种效果在最后幕中展现出特别强烈的冲击力，当时一场扣人心弦的追逐与打斗戏探索了主角的变形。能够呈现不同外貌的可能改变了对抗的动态，并在敌人心中引入了一种偏害妄想，使他们不知下一次攻击将从何而来。动作戏要求密切关注现场的在场人员，因为任何人都有可能化身威胁。这是对超能力的一种富有创意的运用，极具导演和编剧的恐怖片思维特色，通过不确定性来组织危险，而不仅仅是放大破坏的规模。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在其他时刻，身体恐怖则有着更明显的边界。某些场景包含着它们一直在酝酿的暴力，反而在物理痛苦应当全面爆发的时刻减弱了变身的冲击力。对于对该亚流派更熟悉的观众来说，会留有一种影片浅尝辄止、在深入之前便退缩了的遗憾。这种克制并未危及整体的悬疑感，尽管它确实让剧本的一些潜力半途而废。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《泥面人》始终让哈根的痛苦停留在镜头前，即便他的超能力开始威胁到其他人，而瓦特金斯正是利用这种对比为悬疑增添了实质内容。最终的结果表明，当漫画改编作品中的角色不再需要总是履行相同的任务，也不必沦为共享宇宙的为人质时，能够收获多大的提升。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Mike Flanagan e James Watkins utilizam as habilidades de um vilão secundário da DC como recursos de horror corporal e suspense, sem perder de vista o sofrimento do protagonista.

“ Cara-de-Barro ” encontra nos quadrinhos uma oportunidade de explorar o horror corporal sem carregar as obrigações habituais de uma franquia de super-heróis. Com roteiro de Mike Flanagan e direção de James Watkins, dois nomes de destaque do terror atual, a história faz das habilidades do protagonista uma fonte de sofrimento e ameaça. Essa escolha orienta tanto a origem do personagem quanto as sequências de ação, nas quais seus poderes também determinam a maneira de construir o suspense.

O protagonista é Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), ator em ascensão que acaba cruzando o caminho de um chefão mafioso e termina com seu rosto desfigurado. A violência sofrida por ele se agrava ainda mais com a descoberta de quão rapidamente a indústria pode dispensá-lo por perder a aparência. Sem perspectiva de recuperação, ele procura a cientista Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), cujo tratamento clandestino com nanocélulas oferece uma possibilidade de regeneração. A intervenção, porém, impacta seu corpo de uma maneira que ambos são incapazes de controlar.

O roteiro, a direção e a montagem organizam esse percurso em um ritmo bem acelerado. Há informação suficiente para compreender a situação do ator e a urgência de suas escolhas, sem prolongar a exposição ou exigir conhecimento prévio sobre as obras anteriores da DC. Cada tentativa de solucionar um problema produz uma nova dificuldade, dando objetividade ao filme sem torná-lo superficial.

A amargura de Hagen segue presente quando a trama passa a explorar as possibilidades de seus poderes, e isso impede que o horror corporal funcione apenas como uma coleção de imagens repulsivas. O tratamento interfere diretamente na tentativa de retomar sua vida interrompida, e existe uma ironia cruel em submeter alguém já ferido a um procedimento que torna seu corpo ainda mais difícil de controlar.

Tom Rhys Harries é uma peça fundamental no funcionamento do filme, com seu olhar comunicando uma vulnerabilidade que ainda é perceptível quando ele começa a tomar atitudes difíceis de defender. Sua interpretação permite acompanhar essa passagem sem reduzir Hagen a uma vítima passiva ou tornar sua desgraça uma justificativa automática para tudo o que faz.

Naomi Ackie sustenta, como Caitlyn, uma relação que vai além da função de proporcionar o tratamento. A empatia da cientista pelo ator dá peso às consequências de sua intervenção, sem depender de uma mera aproximação romântica. Sua participação mantém o sofrimento de Hagen ligado a alguém que tenta ajudá-lo e também precisa lidar com o que provoca.

Watkins é habilidoso ao utilizar os ambientes claustrofóbicos e os contrastes entre luz e sombra. A iluminação restringe o que pode ser visto e faz dos espaços fechados uma fonte de apreensão, evitando que a ameaça dependa exclusivamente de mostrar o corpo transformado de Hagen. Nos exteriores, a cidade de Gotham não é tão protagonista quanto em “Coringa”, embora sugira com eficiência uma deterioração sem exigir uma apresentação extensa de sua geografia ou de sua mitologia. A cidade serve à atmosfera da história, assim como a escassez de alívios cômicos permite prolongar o desconforto sem interrupções constantes.

O resultado ganha força especial no ato final, quando uma empolgante sequência de perseguição e luta explora a metamorfose do protagonista. A possibilidade de assumir outras aparências altera a dinâmica do confronto e introduz uma paranoia nos inimigos que os deixa sem saber de onde virá o próximo ataque. A ação exige atenção às presenças em cena, pois qualquer pessoa pode se tornar uma ameaça. É um uso criativo dos poderes e bem característico da mentalidade de terror do diretor e do roteirista, organizando o perigo pela incerteza e sem se resumir a ampliar a quantidade de destruição.

Em outros momentos, o horror corporal tem limites mais evidentes. Algumas cenas contêm a violência que vinham preparando, reduzindo o impacto da transformação justamente quando o sofrimento físico deveria ganhar força. Para quem tem maior familiaridade com o subgênero, fica um gostinho de que o filme coloca o pé na água, mas recua antes de mergulhar. A contenção não compromete o suspense do conjunto, embora deixe certas possibilidades da premissa pelo caminho.

“Cara-de-Barro” mantém o sofrimento de Hagen em cena mesmo quando seus poderes passam a ameaçar os demais, e Watkins se vale desse contraste para dar substância ao suspense. O resultado mostra o quanto uma adaptação de quadrinhos pode ganhar quando seus personagens não precisam cumprir sempre as mesmas tarefas — nem ficar reféns de um universo compartilhado.

title_original: IN-DEPENDANCE by IBASHO : The Feminine Gaze
editorial_excerpt_zh: IBASHO 的 IN-DEPENDANCE 带来“女性目光”群展，汇集了当代摄影界四位风格独特的创作者：莉森·斯蒂贝克（Lisen Stibeck）、比吉特·格拉肖普（Birgit Graschopf）、英格丽德·多纳（Ingrid Dorner）…… 本文首次发表在 The…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "IBASHO 的 IN-DEPENDANCE 呈献“女性目光”（The Feminine Gaze），这是一场汇集当代摄影界四位风格独特之声的群展：莉森·斯蒂贝克（Lisen Stibeck）、比吉特·格拉肖普（Birgit Graschopf）、英格丽德·多纳（Ingrid Dorner）和弗洛伦斯·代尔（Florence D’Elle）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为造梦者、艺术家和探索者，这些视觉诗人提出了一种不同的观看方式，不将男性视角视为默认标准。女性目光远不止是一种美学，它是一种不断变幻的视角，不仅质问我们看到了什么，更质问我们是通过谁的眼睛在看。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "女性的力量", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《Un Conte》中，比利时艺术家兼自学成才的作者兼摄影师弗洛伦斯·代尔（Florence D’Elle）拥抱了大画幅摄影和湿版火棉胶摄影的缓慢与物质性，以重访一段极具个人色彩的故事。通过自画像和女儿的影像，她探索了女性在童话象征世界中的地位，取材于一段既沉默又光明、同时也带有暴力印记的过去。受让·科克托（Jean Cocteau）和简·坎皮恩（Jane Campion）的魔幻世界的启发，代尔创造了一个梦幻般的领域，其中的象征手势和母题通向另一重现实。火棉胶工艺固有的不完美成为她视觉语言中不可或缺的一部分，赋予这些影像一种有机、感性且超越时间的质感。借此次展览之机，代尔将推出新书《Opprinnelsen》，该书是她此前在挪威哈尔斯岛（Halsnøy）松霍达兰博物馆（Sunnhordland Museum）驻留创作的成果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "英格丽德·多纳（Ingrid Dorner）是一位居住在慕尼黑的法国艺术家，以其富有感染力、受超现实主义启发而创作的摄影艺术作品而闻名。在本次展览中，多纳呈现了来自三个系列的艺术品：《Liminal》、《Zimmer 23》和《Merveille》。每一部作品都充当了同一运动中的不同阶段——一个内部空间、一个转变的过程以及可能性的重新开启。《Zimmer 23》关乎内部空间。在这里，房间既是一个物理空间，也是一个心理空间：一个充满亲密感、保护感、禁锢感以及时间悬置的地方。《Liminal》占据了门槛。这是一个不稳定的时刻，某种事物不再是它原本的样子，但尚未变成其他东西。在这里，时间、化学作用和人为干预直接作用于摄影材质。转变不仅得到了表现，而且通过名为 mordançage（腐蚀转印法）的摄影工艺在影像内部物理性地发生着。《Merveille》暗示了一种重新开启。它不是对之前的抹去，也不是简单的解决，而是运动、想象力、感官性与可能性的脆弱回归。这三个系列共同构成了一条通往以不同方式观看和栖居世界的可能性的通道。展览期间，多纳将推出由 Hopper&Fuchs 出版的新书《Liminal – La chimie du temps》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "比吉特·格拉肖普（Birgit Graschopf）是一位居住在维也纳的艺术家，她创作神秘、有时带有奇幻色彩摆布的场景，这些场景始终以女性人物为中心，描绘被拍摄人物的内心世界。她的视觉语言借鉴了浪漫主义和超现实主义的手势，在熟悉与亲密、以及陌生与奇诡的氛围之间摇摆。格拉肖普通常会为其黑白摄影作品进行部分手工着色，再加上此前在砂纸或混凝土上手工涂抹感光乳剂的工艺，这增添了绘画般的质感，并极大地塑造了这些影像鲜明的特征。这一工艺的成果始终呈现在她的系列作品《Still/Silence》（2022–2026）中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莉森·斯蒂贝克（Lisen Stibeck）是一位来自瑞典的摄影艺术家，对青少年身份认同和心灵的内心风景有着浓厚兴趣，她通过梦境和原型进行创作，将作品塑造成一种魔幻现实主义的形式。为了“女性目光”展览，斯蒂贝克带来了《A Quiet Distance》，这是一个置于转变状态中的系列，游走于内外部世界之间、存在与消逝之间。该项目探讨了女性目光如何将变化视作一种历经的、直观的、具身的体验，而非一个既定的事件。作品标题指的是所见与所感之间的空间，暗示了一种先于转变发生的静谧觉察。这些作品邀请人们进行一种较慢的观看，一种去倾听而非观看、去感悟而非定义的观看。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览将于 31 月 16:00–20:00 举办开幕酒会，并持续展出至 2026 年 20 月 20 日。四位艺术家将出席见面会。欲了解更多信息，请访问", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "IN-DEPENDANCE by IBASHO Waalsekaai 59 2000 Antwerp, Belgium www.in-dependancegallery.com", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "IN-DEPENDANCE by IBASHO presents The Feminine Gaze , a group exhibition bringing together four distinctive voices in contemporary photography: Lisen Stibeck , Birgit Graschopf , Ingrid Dorner and Florence D’Elle ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As dreamers, artists and explorers, these visual poets propose a different way of seeing, without taking the male perspective as the default. More than an aesthetic, the feminine gaze is a shifting perspective that asks not simply what we see, but through whose eyes we are seeing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The power of women"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Un Conte , Belgian artist and self-taught author-photographer Florence D’Elle embraces the slowness and materiality of large-format photography and wet plate collodion to revisit a deeply personal story. Through self-portraits and images of her daughter, she explores the place of women within the symbolic world of fairy tales, drawing on a past that is silent and luminous, yet also marked by violence. article_text:
IN-DEPENDANCE by IBASHO presents The Feminine Gaze , a group exhibition bringing together four distinctive voices in contemporary photography: Lisen Stibeck , Birgit Graschopf , Ingrid Dorner and Florence D’Elle .

As dreamers, artists and explorers, these visual poets propose a different way of seeing, without taking the male perspective as the default. More than an aesthetic, the feminine gaze is a shifting perspective that asks not simply what we see, but through whose eyes we are seeing.

The power of women

In Un Conte , Belgian artist and self-taught author-photographer Florence D’Elle embraces the slowness and materiality of large-format photography and wet plate collodion to revisit a deeply personal story. Through self-portraits and images of her daughter, she explores the place of women within the symbolic world of fairy tales, drawing on a past that is silent and luminous, yet also marked by violence. Inspired by the magical universes of Jean Cocteau and Jane Campion, D’Elle creates an oneiric realm in which symbolic gestures and motifs open onto another reality. The imperfections inherent to the collodion process become an essential part of her visual language, lending the images an organic, sensual and timeless quality. For the exhibition, D’Elle will launch Opprinnelsen , a book resulting from her artist residency at Sunnhordland Museum on the island of Halsnøy, Norway.

Ingrid Dorner is a French, Munich-based artist known for her evocative, surrealist-inspired photographic artworks. In the exhibition, Dorner presents works from three series: Liminal , Zimmer 23 and Merveille . Each acts as a different step in the same movement – an interior space, a process of transformation and a reopening of possibility. Zimmer 23 is about the interior space. Here, the room becomes both a physical and psychological space: a place of intimacy, protection, confinement and suspended time. Liminal occupies the threshold. It is the unstable moment when something is no longer what it was but has not yet become something else. Here, time, chemistry and manipulation act directly upon the photographic material. Transformation is not only represented, but it also physically takes place within the image via the photographic process called mordançage. Merveille suggests a reopening. Not an erasure of what came before, nor a simple resolution, but the fragile return of movement, imagination, sensuality and possibility. Together, the three series form a passage towards the possibility of seeing and inhabiting the world differently. During the exhibition, Dorner will present her newly published book Liminal – La chimie du temps by Hopper&Fuchs.

Birgit Graschopf is a Vienna-based artist who creates mysterious, sometimes whimsically staged scenes that always place female figures at the centre, depicting inner worlds of the photographed characters. Referencing gestures from Romanticism and Surrealism, her visual language oscillates between an atmosphere of what’s familiar and intimate, as well as what’s foreign and uncanny. Often, Graschopf colours her black-and-white photographs partially by hand, which, together with the prior manual application of photo emulsion on sandpaper or concrete, adds a painterly aspect and significantly contributes to the distinctive character of the images. The result of this process is ever-present in her series titled Still/Silence (2022–2026).

Lisen Stibeck is a photographic artist from Sweden with a keen interest in teenage identity and the inner landscape of the psyche, working with dreams and archetypes, shaping her work into a form of magical realism. For The Feminine Gaze , Stibeck presents A Quiet Distance , a series situated in a state of transformation, between inner and outer worlds, between presence and disappearance. This project explores how the feminine gaze perceives change as a lived, intuitive, embodied experience rather than a defined event. The title refers to the space between what is seen and what is felt, suggesting a quiet awareness that precedes transformation. The works invite a slower gaze, one that listens rather than looks and senses rather than defines.

The exhibition opens with a vernissage on 31 October from 16:00–20:00 and will run until 20 December 2026. The four artists will be present for a meet & greet. For more information, visit

IN-DEPENDANCE by IBASHO Waalsekaai 59 2000 Antwerp, Belgium www.in-dependancegallery.com

article_text:
Italian neorealist master Roberto Rossellini , though he died in 1977, turns 120 this year. In celebration, major retrospective series are coming up.

Film Forum in New York, the Italian Ministry of Culture, and Cinecittà will present “Rossellini 120,” a 25- film retrospective dedicated to Roberto Rossellini, opening at Film Forum on November 20. The retrospective will also open in Los Angeles on November 4 at the Academy Museum as “Roberto Rossellini Prefers Real Life,” courtesy of the Italian Ministry of Culture and Cinecittà.

Through December 10, New York’s Film Forum will host the 25-film “Rossellini 120.” The filmmaker’s daughter, Oscar-nominated actress Isabella Rossellini, will appear in person on November 20 with “Voyage to Italy” (which starred her mother, Ingrid Bergman, opposite George Sanders) and again on November 26 (i.e., Thanksgiving) with “Flowers of St. Francis” and “Europa ’51.” IndieWire shares exclusive details as well as a trailer for the retrospective above. The program is a partnership of Film Forum, Cinecittà, and the Italian Ministry of Culture

Rossellini is best known for his films with his third wife, Ingrid Bergman, including “Stromboli,” “Europe ’51,” “Fear,” “Journey to Italy,” and “Joan of Arc at the Stake.”

Isabella said, “Our family is coming en masse to see the retrospective at Film Forum. It’s an occasion for my sister Ingrid and I to show the films to the youngest family members, who never met their Nonno (grandfather) or bisnonno (great-grandfather), in the 120th year since his birth. We’re super-grateful to both Film Forum and Cinecittà, who for years have restored and presented our father’s work. His films continue to inspire filmmakers all around the world.”

The program includes Rossellini films “Rome, Open City,” “Paisan,” “Germany, Year Zero.” The lineup also includes Guy Maddin’s “My Dad Is 100 Years Old,” featuring Isabella Rossellini, and the documentaries “Viva Ingrid!” by Alessandro Rossellini and “Rossellini Through His Own Eyes” by Adriano Aprà.

Manuela Cacciamani, CEO of Cinecittà, added, “Film Forum has long been one of New York’s most beloved homes for repertory cinema, a place where generations of audiences have discovered the great masters of world film. It is the ideal setting for the work of Roberto Rossellini, who changed the language of cinema and whose films continue to speak powerfully to our present. Cinecittà has held the rights to ten of his most representative films for thirty years, restored in our own laboratories and preserved in valuable 35mm prints, which we are delighted to make exceptionally available for this occasion, that follows the steps of many joint past initiatives, like the legendary 1993 ‘Tutto Fellini.’ We thank our U.S. partners Janus Films and The Criterion Collection for their care in distributing Rossellini’s legacy through the years”.

Film Forum audiences will also see Cinecittà’s new 4K restoration of “Fear” from 1954, which was Rossellini’s last film with Bergman. The Film Forum series arrives a couple of weeks after the launch of “Rossellini Prefers Real Life” at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles, beginning November 4. Isabella and family will also be in attendance for that series, which includes the above films for West Coasters.

article_text:
Mit Aktionen wie "Bitte liebt Österreich" brachte Christoph Schlingensief gesellschaftliche Konflikte auf die Bühne – und sein Publikum gegen sich auf. Nun ist sein Werk in Berlin zu sehen. Wir verlosen Freitickets

Christoph Schlingensief machte aus Politik Kunst, und aus Kunst Politik. Als im Jahr 2000 die rechtspopulistische FPÖ in Österreich an die Regierung kam, stellte er vor der Wiener Staatsoper einen Container mit angeblichen Asylbewerbern auf. Kameras überwachten die Bewohner, das Publikum durfte im Internet darüber abstimmen, wer abgeschoben werden sollte. "Bitte liebt Österreich" hieß die Aktion. War das nun Kunst, politische Aufklärung oder einfach geschmacklos? Bei Schlingensief ließ sich das selten eindeutig beantworten.

Ohnehin machte der 2010 verstorbene Künstler wenig Unterschied zwischen Bühne und Wirklichkeit, wie der Gropius Bau jetzt zeigt. Die Ausstellung "Es ist nicht mehr mein Problem!", die zuvor im Wiener MAK Station machte , vereint Filmaufnahmen, Installationen und rekonstruierte Schauplätze, die Einblick in ein Schaffen zwischen Theater, Film und bildender Kunst geben. Mal sollten Arbeitslose den Wolfgangsee zum Überlaufen bringen, um Helmut Kohls Ferienhaus zu fluten, mal standen ausstiegswillige Neonazis in seiner "Hamlet"-Inszenierung auf der Bühne. Und für die Fernsehsendung "Freakstars 3000" entwickelte er mit Menschen mit Behinderungen eine ziemlich eigenwillige Antwort auf die Castingshow-Kultur.

Aino Laberenz, Bühnen- und Kostümbildnerin, Nachlassverwalterin und Leiterin des Operndorfs Afrika, beschreibt Schlingensief im Monopol-Podcast "Kunst und Leben" als "einen Künstler in Bewegung, der alles aufgenommen hat wie ein Schwamm". Statt Antworten zu liefern, habe er sein Publikum zum Mitdenken und Mitmachen herausgefordert. Seine Kunst sei nie Selbstzweck gewesen.

Monopol verlost 5 × 2 Tickets für die Ausstellung "Es ist nicht mehr mein Problem!" im Gropius Bau in Berlin. Für die Teilnahme schicken Sie bitte eine E-Mail mit Ihrem Vor- und Nachnamen und dem Betreff "Christoph Schlingensief" bis Donnerstag, 29. Oktober, 14 Uhr, an info@monopol-magazin.de . Die Gewinnerinnen und Gewinner werden per E-Mail benachrichtigt. Der Rechtsweg ist ausgeschlossen.

article_text:
Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “ Once Upon a Time in the Middle East .” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a summer box office hit at home — makes for an extravagant display of the strength of the nation’s commercial film industry. Strength, in the sense that no modest operation could conceivably pull off the technical wizardry and large-scale worldbuilding showcased here, where an entire city is at one point turned into an inferno of crumbling buildings, and a massive military base is, in a later scene, ambushed in a rain of blazing pyrotechnics.

Related Stories

Jennifer Lawrence Filmed a Nude Scene and Discovered Crew Members Who Were Not Approved to Be on Set: 'I Came Down Hard on That'

The film is also, as expected from this state-backed production, blatantly propagandistic — but in a way that is particularly baffling, and shockingly tasteless. If those sound like the elements for a good time, in the B-movie sense, then you are also correct. Against the odds, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is also, both regrettably and miraculously, extremely watchable. The Jekyll part of your brain will tell you to leave but the Hyde-side will keep you seated in morbid, twitchy-eyed fascination over the film’s two-and-a-half hour runtime.

To cut straight to the point, this is a film in which China symbolically emerges from the rubble of the Iraq War as a pacifistic patriarch and guardian of all the world’s children. Director Wen Muyue delivers this subtext through the story of Xu Fu (Shen Teng), a debt-ridden chef who agrees to temporarily take over a Chinese restaurant in the fictional Gulf-region city of Bahata, intending to return to his daughter and mother in China in two years time.

Flash-forwards to an elder Xu Fu with liver spots and a conspicuous scar on his cheek tell us that he will indeed make it back to his family, but it’ll take much longer than a few years — the frankly absurd reasons for his delay a consequence of his, let’s say, geopolitical misfortunes. He’s a man in the wrong place at the wrong time, though, cleverly, the film makes the point that a good Chinese meal is never unwelcome. In fact it’s globally in demand — a lifeline that ensures Xu Fu’s survival through the film’s whirlwind of events.

Before we get to the grisly images of dead children covered in ash, the film starts out as a feel-good dramedy in which Xu Fu adapts to his new surroundings. Frazzled softie Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), the restaurant manager, is our hero’s bridge between China and his new home, translating for Xu Fu between Arabic and Chinese during tense but diplomatic discussions with the restaurant owner Zaid (Sherif Sabby). Glossy, mouthwatering closeups of grilled meats and bubbling stone-pot stews testify to the success of Xu Fu’s kitchen takeover. Nurturing local talent is also on the agenda when he takes on a mentee, Seif (Omar Sharif — no, not that one), an angsty orphan who learns to sublimate his rage into the art of Chinese cooking. Though as the film goes on, this anger grows into a furious, war-hardened desire for retribution. Does a delicious roasted duck stand a chance? It does, in this film’s mind, with the help of the preternaturally compassionate Xu Fu.

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is something of a both-sides film in that both the Americans and the not-so-thinly-veiled Iraqis are gross caricatures of themselves, and there’s particular ire reserved for that most treacherous of abominations: Chinese-American … food. In epic-handshake-meme solidarity, Xu Fu and Zaid agree that their restaurant will never serve U.S.-style Chinese dishes like General Tso’s chicken; and when the US troops bomb Bahata to smithereens and occupy the city, a crass Chinese-American private (Aarif Lee Zhi-ting) bullies his way into free meals at Xu Fu’s restaurant. Not a pushover but a practical-minded realist, the chef takes the punches, striking up a booze-smuggling deal with the Americans to keep the orphans living in his restaurant safe.

The maddening implausibility that sustains the film’s relentless, weirdly hypnotizing forward momentum means we’re never in one place — or one mood — for too long. Zaid’s home is bombed in one intensely melodramatic sequence that culminates in a slow zoom over Zaid cradling his dead wife and child. Next thing we know, he’s radicalized and joins a terrorist group. Xu Fu, Ma Junsheng and Seif — the cooking trio — are promptly captured by the U.S. Army and forced to preside over the kitchen on base. This allows for more sumptuous shots of delicious food while Xu Fu is, for whatever reason, targeted by an aggro, block-jawed American soldier. Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng also play surrogate dads to Seif, whose increasingly violent eruptions threaten to change the course of his life more than once.

For all its dewy-eyed sentimentality, the film is also startlingly brutal and bloody, making for a deranged whiplash effect that’s felt most powerfully in the film’s final act, which is set in a terrorist stronghold where pipsqueaks are brainwashed into becoming suicide bombers. Cozy, brotherly scenes (as when Ma Junsheng slips Seif a smuggled can of soda) are directly followed by executions and montages of plush-bear-wielding kiddies invoking jihad. There’s a slickness to the carnage that rubs uncomfortably against the film’s humanist ethos, rendering artificial (for all Shen Teng’s trembling and mouth-contorting labors) the horrific tragedies that befall its characters. It’s a vision of wartime brutality that’s both blithely matter-of-fact and desperate to pull at our heartstrings; utterly delusional, in other words, and hard to look away from.

article_text:
California’s $750 million bet on Hollywood has not reversed the overall decline in production, according to data released Wednesday by FilmLA .

Instead, production levels fell 3.7% in the third quarter — even as the share of projects receiving state subsidies continued to rise. Location shoots remain well below the five-year average.

State officials had hoped that the dramatic expansion of the state’s film and TV tax credit last year would show stronger results by now. After an encouraging first quarter of 2026, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass declared that the industry was “turning a corner.”

But the number of shoot days has declined in both quarters since then, suggesting that the magnitude of the state tax credit was simply not enough to offset the forces behind the decline.

In a statement on Wednesday, Bass nevertheless highlighted “encouraging signs of progress,” noting that the share of scripted projects receiving state subsidies has nearly doubled since last year.

“These gains show that incentives work, but we must do more,” Bass said, reiterating her support for an unlimited state incentive.

Her opponent in the upcoming mayoral election, Nithya Raman, has faulted Bass for not doing more to help the industry, and has also called eliminating the cap on the state subsidy.

In 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom led the move to increase the state’s film and TV incentive from $330 million per year to $750 million. The California Film Commission saw an immediate jump in applications after the increase took effect on July 1, 2025, with the expectation that those projects would go into production in early 2026.

While the expansion has not reversed the decline in total production volume, it has led to a measurable increase in the share of L.A. shows receiving tax credits. According to FilmLA, 40.2% of scripted shows filming in the last quarter received the state tax credit — nearly double the figure from a year ago.

In TV comedy, some 62% of shows received the credit — up from 19% in 2025 — while in TV dramas the share increased from 21% to 49%.

On the bright side, TV comedy recorded its best quarter since the 2023 strikes by the Writers Guild of America and SAG-AFTRA, with 192 shoot days, up from 57 in the prior three months. But that increase was more than offset by a decline in TV dramas from 732 shoot days to 494. Reality TV also continued to struggle with 630 shoot days, 66% below the five-year average.

“Obviously we’re disappointed to see the numbers down overall,” said Philip Sokoloski, a VP at FilmLA, though he noted that some of the state-supported categories did see an increase. “The fact remains that work that does not receive incentive support is increasingly likely to leave California for places that are more affordable.”

The upcoming Netflix film “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is among the rare big-budget projects to shoot in L.A., thanks to $20 million in state tax credits.

“I hope that it comes back to this city, because it’s what the city feels like it’s for,” Elizabeth Debicki, one of the film’s co-stars, told Variety on Wednesday. “The crew, the people who live here — they want to work here. So that was a joy.”

Marc Malkin contributed to this story.

article_text:
U npacking assorted tubs of carrot sticks and salad, Keira Knightley winces apologetically. “I just realised I’ve got very crunchy food,” she says. How apropos that she should consider the impact that her lunch might have on my audio recording when we are here to discuss The Lives of Others , a new play in which the characters are divided between the spies and the spied-upon.

Based on the Oscar-winning 2006 film and set in East Berlin in 1984, the play stars Knightley as Christa-Maria, a theatre actor in a relationship with a playwright, Georg, played by Luke Thompson. Earwigging on them is Wiesler (Stephen Dillane), the Stasi officer whose principles are gradually challenged and weakened by his round-the-clock exposure to this cultured couple.

Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s original movie opens with an interrogation scene in which a persecuted citizen is grilled relentlessly for 40 hours – the length of time it takes, according to Wiesler, for a suspect to crack under questioning. I have only been allotted one-fortieth of that time with Knightley and Thompson, who has brought along his own leafy lunch to the north London town hall where rehearsals are under way. But I am still hopeful of extracting a few details about what the play’s visionary writer-director Robert Icke has up his sleeve. This is the man who introduced Sliding Doors-style alternate-reality scenes into Romeo and Juliet , put a countdown clock on stage in Oedipus (and others), and added the Beach Boys to Oresteia .

Interrogation techniques turn out not to be necessary today. “It’s quite a technical show,” volunteers Thompson, the 38-year-old Bridgerton star who worked with Icke previously on Hamlet ( with Andrew Scott as the Prince ) and Oresteia. “Rather than different scenes, it’s like one big set-piece with people coming in and passing batons. It’s almost musical.” Which is odd, laughs the 41-year-old Knightley, “because Rob hates dancing. He is not a man who dances.”

She has some beans of her own to spill. “We’re on a revolving stage,” she says, “so we’re always on the move.” This will enable the audience to see Christa-Maria and Georg at the same time as their Stasi eavesdropper. Thompson believes this lends the stage version an advantage over the movie: “Bringing a story about watching into the theatre is maybe even better, because the audience is literally peering in on what’s happening. Whereas in a film, there’s the barrier of the screen.”

Only when I ask whether they are using the play’s new Max Richter score during rehearsals does Thompson become remotely tight-lipped: “I don’t know if I’m allowed to say that.” Knightley throws caution to the wind: “We are using it in rehearsal, yeah. It’s very beautiful. Everyone’s in the room: we’ve got the sound designer, the costume designer, the video designer …” Video, eh? Another hint. Icke used screens in the penetrating version of Orwell’s 1984 which he co-adapted with Duncan Macmillan; in his Hamlet, the Ghost turned up on CCTV. It’s a convention that risks seeming passe now. “Video can feel gimmicky,” Thompson concedes. “But it’s relevant here because it’s all about surveillance.”

The nature of surveillance in society has changed markedly, even in the two decades since the movie opened. “You want there to be a camera at the bus stop when your bag’s been nicked,” reflects Knightley, displaying a touching faith in police priorities. “You feel safer because of that surveillance. But then you ask: ‘Who is surveying me?’”

In the same year that The Lives of Others was released, she became part of the first wave of public figures to discover that their phone messages had been hacked by tabloids. How far has that helped her understand the sort of paranoia that dominates the play? “I do have a personal experience of what that is. Then again, I knew that my phone was being hacked because I had something tangible to show for it. There were stories. Or for me, it was mostly pictures. I knew I was being followed and then I could see that I was being followed. I didn’t feel like I was going mad. Whereas the characters are in a funny world where they don’t know when or if they’re being monitored.”

Modern parallels have been part of the rehearsal room discussions. I mention the likelihood that visitors to the US now have their social media accounts probed at immigration, and Knightley’s eyes light up. “Ah, but did that ever happen?” she asks. “Or is it enough that you say it’s going to happen for people to self-censor? You don’t even have to follow through on the threat. You just have to put it out there.” Thompson agrees: “It’s what’s so clever and efficient about the Stasi. The best way to create surveillance is for people to do it themselves.” And not only through self-censorship: estimates are that there was one informant for every 6.5 citizens in East Germany.

Top of the cast’s reading list for the play is Stasiland, Anna Funder’s 2003 account of life in the GDR. Funder has called Von Donnersmarck’s film “superb” but also “a fantasy narrative that could not have taken place (and never did) under the GDR dictatorship”. The Lives of Others, she wrote in 2007, “doesn’t accurately portray the way totalitarian systems work, because it needs to leave room for its hero to act humanely (something such systems are designed to prevent).” Another of her charges is that the movie inadvertently legitimised the ongoing campaign by former Stasi agents to launder their reputation.

In at least one documented instance, however, the movie has had a real-world benefit. In 2014 , 43 veterans of an elite, clandestine Israeli military intelligence unit withdrew from participating in “the state’s actions against Palestinians”, protesting that their government was guilty of “political persecution” in refusing to distinguish “between Palestinians who are and are not involved in violence”. One Israeli whistleblower singled out The Lives of Others as the catalyst for his own awakening. He and his colleagues, he realised, “were similar to the kind of oppressive intelligence in oppressive regimes”.

Not everyone regards von Donnersmarck’s picture as a force for good. When a journalist recommended it to the actor Julie Christie in 2007, she replied: “I’m not sure I can bear to see a film they gave the Oscar to, that tells you what awful people communists are.” Thompson mulls this over. “There are characters who are mouthpieces for something along those lines,” he says. “But it’s not just a politics play. Part of the fun, I think, is that the characters are mysterious and you never know quite which way they’re going to go. If what audiences take from the play is ‘Communists are awful’, then I’d feel like we’d failed.”

Audiences can take what they like from it – as long as they don’t take photographs. It was the sight of phone cameras being whipped out for the curtain call at Icke’s Oedipus that sent its star, Lesley Manville, into a huff. (“Clap or don’t clap,” she later said, “but don’t just stick your phone in our face.”) Despite starring on stage in Ivo van Hove’s four-hour adaptation of Hanya Yanagihara’s A Little Life , where a phone ban failed to prevent the leaking of nude snaps of his co-star James Norton , Thompson trusts the audience. “I think people broadly follow the no-phone rule,” he says. Knightley may not have set foot on stage for 11 years (“Small children, no sleep” is her pithy explanation for the hiatus) but, as a punter, she notes approvingly the “absolute fucking fury from everyone if somebody’s phone goes off in the theatre”.

I wonder how they both feel about the standing ovations which have become ubiquitous to the point of meaningless at West End productions. Knightley thinks ticket prices might explain it. “I took my kids to see a musical recently and we really did enjoy it, but it cost so much that I was, like, ‘We are going to love this!’” With tickets for The Lives of Others peaking at £225, she and Thompson can expect to see audiences springing to their feet every night.

“In a strange way, though, the exchange that happens between actors and an audience during the clapping is the least important or interesting moment of it,” says Thompson. “If people see something good, it stays with them. Perhaps we’ve been missing that – and that’s why people get so excited.”

“I like your optimism,” says Knightley, clearing away the lunchtime detritus. “There’s me going, ‘Maybe it’s because the tickets are expensive.’ And you’re like, ‘It’s because the play transports you!’”

The Lives of Others is at the Adelphi theatre, London , from 14 October until 9 January

article_text:
AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater , which will shutter on Jan. 3.

Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with any of AMC’s alternatives to share the space. In addition to the 15-screen AMC theater, the building also houses a Fairway supermarket and bank, which are also expected to close.

“Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease,” Aron writes. “We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.”

Popular on Variety

On Aug. 24, Variety reported that the Kips Bay theater would close at the end of 2026, ending a 27-year run at the location. AMC took over the theater in 2006, which became the chain’s second-largest multiplex in the city (after Times Square’s Empire 25 theater). The Kips Bay location has become adored by local residents, who staged a protest in September in an attempt to stop the closure.

“Every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15,” Aron wrote. “It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theaters across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theaters operated by AMC nationally.”

The theater closure comes after a r ecord-breaking summer box office , which saw movies like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and more collectively gross $4.67 billion domestically. There are also major upcoming movies like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III,” which Kips Bay residents will now still get a chance to see at their beloved theater before it closes for good.

Read Aron’s full letter below.

“To the Kips Bay Community,

Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.

So many moviegoers and neighbors, and importantly so many of your elected officials, have rallied around our theatre. (Given the central role that movie theatres play in the lives of so many New Yorkers, perhaps it is much better and more accurate to say that so many of you have rallied around YOUR theatre.)

On behalf of everyone at AMC, thank you. Your support means a great deal to us, and especially to our theatre team members at AMC Kips Bay 15 who work tirelessly day-in and day-out to put smiles on your faces.

In thinking about this theatre, which has been a cultural icon and entertainment lifeline to so many nearby residents for decades and decades since its opening on May 14 1999, I want to make one thing absolutely clear:

AMC Theatres does not want to go. Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay.

Operating under long term leases, there was a time that the monies headed each month to the theatre’s landlord had risen to become so high that the theatre’s long-term viability was uncertain. But, we were fortunate to have been successful in addressing those concerns in recent years. Today this theatre (one which has been in continuous operation for more than 25 years) has a bright future — if we would be allowed to keep it.

Indeed, every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15. It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theatres across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theatres operated by AMC nationally.

In that light, this is a theatre that should not be even close to a permanent shutting off of its lights.

Of course, AMC wants this AMC movie theatre to stay in place.

And remembering how much and how often Americans love watching movies in theatres, a tradition in Manhattan that dates back more than a full century, we have heard from so many of you that you too want us to stay open for your benefit.

Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours.

Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.

We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.

We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.

It isn’t true that New Yorkers can be prevented from having your cake and eating it too. Indeed you can. But only if people of goodwill think out of the box a bit. After all, the ubiquitous proverb “where there is a will, there is a way” is one that is believed to have first been published in the year 1640 — that’s three hundred eighty six years back to be precise.

Speaking of people of goodwill, I especially want to express gratitude to Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal and New York State Assembly Member Keith Powers, for their leadership and tireless advocacy on this matter. Reinforcing and speaking for the local community’s clear desire, they have energetically brought attention to the importance of keeping an AMC movie theatre open and operating in Kips Bay.

In summary, this is a theatre that you in Kips Bay want to continue to be at your beck and call, and one that we at AMC unequivocally also want to be allowed to continue within our theatrical fleet.

But time is short. Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.

Hopefully, there is an outcome in which a wise workable solution is devised, one that will benefit and please the entire neighborhood. What say you NYU Langone Health?

Whatever happens, I want you to know how much AMC appreciates your support, your efforts and your voice. We are proud to have been part of the Kips Bay community since 1999, and I sincerely hope that we can continue to be part of it for years to come.

Sincerely, Adam Aron, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer AMC Entertainment

article_text:
Harry Styles has invited one of the buzziest documentary filmmakers on the market behind the curtain of his historic Madison Square Garden residency.

John Wilson , the director behind indie box-office surprise “The History of Concrete” and HBO’s “How To with John Wilson,” has been rolling cameras on Styles at MSG since August, two sources with knowledge of the project said.

Related Stories

YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom

YouTube to Label AI-Generated Songs Across Its Platforms: Listeners ‘Want Transparency’

Wilson is capturing footage for a doc expected to be a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world. One source described it as featuring authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.

Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles produced the project. UPCG will own global rights to the film. Though distribution plans are still being worked out, insiders said the doc may be positioned for a theatrical release via Universal.

Popular on Variety

Styles is currently in the midst of the largest single-engagement residency ever at MSG, part of his “Together, Together” tour. It began in late August and is set to run through the end of October. The show has created plenty of viral moments and provided ample short-shorts . Reps for the singer, Wilson, and Universal had no immediate comment. Social media lit up over the weekend thanks to a fan-snapped photo of Wilson trailing styles with a camera.

Wilson’s got a knack for interrogating the mundane, as well as highlighting the absurdity of humans and the levers that make them work. He may seem an out-of-the-box choice for a glossy pop music documentary, but not if you’re paying attention to current sensibilities. Look at Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, whose Elizabeth Holmes project “You Can See Everything” is burning up the specialty box office this weekend. Fielder started in the realm of absurdist comedy, and with the Holmes project moves into a world of watercooler high crimes and compelling fourth-wall breaking. Billie Eilish recruited “Titanic ” and “Avatar” mastermind James Cameron to direct her own theatrical concert opus “Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour,” which was released in theaters this summer.

Wilson began his career directing music videos. He is repped by UTA.

article_text:
Few cultural figures embody the 2026 film industry better than Curry Barker . After writing and directing one of the year’s biggest box office hits in “ Obsession ,” Barker became the face of a new group of young filmmakers who took nontraditional paths to Hollywood and are helping bring Gen Z audiences to theaters. It made him a natural choice to receive IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award at our Los Angeles Summit on Saturday, October 17.

During the event, Barker sat down with IndieWire’s VP, editorial strategy Chris O’Falt for a wide-ranging conversation about his process, career, and advice for young filmmakers hoping to follow a similar path.

Barker discussed moving from Alabama to Los Angeles, where he met his future collaborator Cooper Tomlinson. The two soon dropped out of film school to focus on making short films for their That’s a Bad Idea YouTube channel. The road eventually led him to make “Obsession” and his upcoming feature “Anything But Ghosts,” which had already wrapped before “Obsession” took the box office by storm. Both films are original ideas — though he cautioned that the “lessons” to be learned from his success have more to do with the value of quality storytelling than audiences preferring one type of film over another.

“I can only speak to what makes me go to the theater,” Barker said. “I think the lesson to be learned is that we crave good stories. And that doesn’t necessarily mean IP. But it also doesn’t necessarily mean original. Like if an original movie fails, the lesson shouldn’t be that originals don’t work and we go back to IP. The lesson should be ‘Oh, this movie probably sucked.’”

Barker also expressed his optimism about cinema’s future as a medium thanks to an influx of theater attendance from younger audiences. He even offered his own theories about why Gen Z has become our largest ticket-buying demographic.

“Maybe we’re all just tired of being in our house on our phones, and COVID was horrible,” he said. “The theater is just a cool place! It’s perfect for Gen Z, because you’re going to have social interactions, but you’re not expected to talk to anybody. You can just put your phone away for two hours and have a collective experience with humans without having to talk to them!”

Watch the complete conversation with Barker in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here .

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "舞乐装束以左方的红、金以及右方的青、银为基调色彩，是将担任舞蹈角色的宫廷武官制服进行了华丽改造的产物。舞乐不仅在宫廷中，在有影响力的寺社中也盛极一时，作为高野山镇守社天野社（丹生都比売神社）传世的装束，留存下了尽情运用14～15世纪染织技术的富有魅力的设计作品。起因于应仁之乱（1467～77）的战国混乱给雅乐带来了沉重打击，但经由朝廷与权力者得以复兴，不久后受到统制。随着这一点，装束在宫廷及东西主要寺社中也收敛为共通性极高的设计。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一面貌可以通过将悠久舞乐传统传承至今的大阪四天王寺装束，以及时隔约40年公开的栃木轮王寺藏珍品等一睹为快。不妨来尽情领略跨越时空流传至今、装点舞乐的装束之美吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "天明釜（现栃木县佐野市）的特征是自由的造型与古朴的肌理。本作因向外张开的口部造型酷似十王中阎魔大王等的冠帽形状，故被称为“十王口”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "跨越千数百年的时光传承至今的雅乐与舞乐。本展中，从高野山天野社流传下来的中世纪染织珍贵遗物，到与丰臣家颇有渊源的四天王寺装束，以及时隔约40年公开的德川将军家调进的轮王寺装束，将齐聚一堂。纤细的织造、鲜艳的刺绣以及堂堂剪裁中所寄托的美意识，无遗漏地传达了日本染织史的精华。此外，不妨结合同时举办的白描画与开炉茶道具展，以及11月中旬迎来最佳观赏期的根津美术馆特有的美丽庭园红叶漫步，在这个艺术之秋，尽情饱满地享受日本丰富的传统文化与深秋的情趣吧。（美术展导航）", article_text:
根津美術館で特別展「舞楽装束 ―受け継がれる染織の美―」が10月24日に開幕し、11月23日まで開催されています。中世から近世初期にさかのぼる染織品が、保存が難しく失われやすいにもかかわらず、奇跡的な状態で全国から集結しています。

14〜15世紀にさかのぼる高野山の金剛峯寺や、その鎮守社である天野社（ 丹生都比売 神社）伝来品から、天下統一を果たした豊臣家の文化事業として寄進された大阪・四天王寺の「太平楽装束」、約40年ぶりに公開となる徳川家光が寄進した日光山輪王寺の装束まで、全国の歴史的な装束の名品が一堂に会する奇跡の空間でした。

変わらないものの中にある変化

長い伝統をもつ舞楽は、変わらないことが本質と言えるかもしれません。ところが、本展の醍醐味は、伝統に潜む「変遷」の歴史です。例えば、胸と背を覆う「 裲襠 」装束を見ると、1378年銘など中世の作例は深いV字型なのに対し、近世以降は首元が詰まった立ち襟・丸首型へと変化しています。

また、演目「崑崙八仙」の意匠も変化していました。中世の古図では「苔の衣」だったのが、近世には「波に鯉と網」へと衣装の柄が大きく変わっています。型を守りつつも、時代ごとの美意識を重ねてきたからこそ、舞楽は時を超えて受け継がれてきたのだと実感させる展示でした。（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班 岡本公樹）

特別展「舞楽装束 ―受け継がれる染織の美―」

会場：根津美術館（東京都港区南青山6-5-1）

会期：2026年10月24日［土］～11月23日［月・祝］

開館時間：午前10時～午後5時（最終入館 午後4時30分）

休館日：毎週月曜日（11月23日［月・祝］は開館）

観覧料（日時指定予約制）： ・オンライン日時指定予約：一般 1600円／学生（大学生以上） 700円 ・当日券（根津美術館受付で販売）：一般 1800円／学生（大学生以上） 900円 ※オンライン予約者を優先案内。当日券は購入まで待機の可能性あり 混雑状況によっては当日券を販売中止 ※障害者手帳提示者及び同伴者1名は上記料金から200円引き ※高校生以下は無料（学生証要提示）

アクセス： 地下鉄銀座線・半蔵門線・千代田線〈表参道〉駅下車 ・A5出口（階段）より徒歩8分 ・B4出口（階段とエスカレータ）より徒歩10分 ・B3出口（エレベータまたはエスカレータ）より徒歩10分

詳細は、 根津美術館公式サイト まで。

根津美術館（東京都港区）で、特別展「舞楽装束 ―受け継がれる染織の美―」が10月24日から11月23日まで開催されています。

外来の楽や舞を取り込みながら独自の発展を遂げた日本の古典芸能・雅楽。そのうち舞を伴うのが舞楽です。雅楽は、日本古来の 歌舞 と5世紀より中国や朝鮮半島を経由して日本にもたらされたアジア各国の楽舞が融合して原形が成立しました。その後宮廷芸能として盛んになり、10世紀には、雑多に併存していた楽舞を中国系の 左方 ［ 左舞 ・ 唐楽 ］と朝鮮半島系の 右方 ［ 右舞 ・ 高麗楽 ］の二つの系統に大別する整理が進みました。こうして日本独自の演出法が定められ、現在につながる形式が整えられます。

舞楽装束は、左方は赤・金、右方は青・銀を基調色として、舞の担い手であった宮廷武官の制服を華やかに変化させたものです。舞楽は宮廷のみならず有力な寺社でも盛んにおこなわれ、高野山の鎮守社である天野社（ 丹生都比売 神社）伝来の装束には、14～15世紀の染織技術を駆使した魅力的なデザインの作例が残されています。応仁の乱（1467～77）に端を発する戦国の混乱により雅楽は大打撃を受けますが、朝廷や権力者によって復興、やがて統制されます。それにつれて装束も、宮廷ならびに東西の主要寺社では共通性の高いデザインに収斂していきます。

この様子を、悠久の舞楽の伝統を今に受け継ぐ大阪・四天王寺の装束、そして約40年ぶりに公開される栃木・輪王寺蔵の優品などを通じて見ることができます。時を超えて今日まで守り伝えられた舞楽を彩る装束の美を堪能してみてはいかがでしょうか。

高野山天野社の舞楽装束―中世染織のタイムカプセル―

舶来の金 襴 を贅沢に用いた 毛縁 の襴。裏地の墨書から、永和4年（1378）に「高野山 丹生 社」（天野社）へ施入されたことが知られます。装束の完全な形を保つ点と合わせ、基準作としてきわめて重要です。

脇が縫われていない 貫頭衣 である 裲襠 を身体に固定するために、腰の位置に締める帯。裏地に「貞和三年丁亥八月三日」の墨書があり、製作年代の下限を伝える貴重な作品です。

舞楽の演目「羅陵王」（陵王とも）を舞う童子を描いたやまと絵の小品。赤い 袍 の上に牡丹模様の金襴襴と襴帯、亀甲模様の括袴を着用しており、装束が実際にどのように身に着けられたかがわかります。面をつけず 天冠 を戴くのは 童舞 であることを示します。

四天王寺の舞楽装束―天下統一を果たした豊臣家の文化事業―

大阪・四天王寺の舞楽は、同寺と深いかかわりを持つ 天王寺楽所 の楽人によって古くから行われてきました。天正4年（1576）、四天王寺は兵火により焼失し舞楽用具も失われますが、豊臣家による寄進によって再興されました。このような盛衰を経ながらも、聖徳太子の御霊を慰める「 聖霊会 」などの法要で現在も奏され続けています。舞楽「太平楽」は「聖霊会」の法要の部の終わりを告げる舞として欠かすことのできない演目で、その装束には甲冑や武器など10を超えるアイテムが含まれます。

同時開催展

展示室5 白描の美

墨の細線を主とする白描画。中世以前の仏教図像や絵巻の下絵、近世のやまと絵、さらに近代画まで、静謐なモノクロームの美を堪能できます。

嵯峨に 六条御息所 を訪ね、別れを惜しむ光源氏。近世の白描は、墨の濃淡や抑揚のある線、あるいは金なども導入して表現の幅を広げました。

展示室6 開炉 ―冬を迎える―

11月、茶室では炉を開き、冬を迎えるために席中を一新します。一年の節目となる祝儀の茶会にふさわしく、格式高い茶道具を取り合せます。

天明釜（現在の栃木県佐野市）は、自由な形と 侘 びた肌合いが特徴。本作は、外に開く口作りが、十王の 閻魔 大王などの冠の形に似ていることから「十王口」と称されます。

千数百年の時を超えて受け継がれてきた雅楽と舞楽。本展では、高野山天野社に伝わる中世染織の貴重な遺品から、豊臣家ゆかりの四天王寺装束、そして約40年ぶりの公開となる徳川将軍家調進の輪王寺装束までが一堂に会します。繊細な織りや鮮やかな刺繍、堂々たる仕立てに宿る美意識は、日本の染織史の精華を余すところなく伝えてくれます。さらに同時開催の白描画や開炉の茶道具展示、そして11月中旬から見ごろを迎える根津美術館ならではの美しい庭園の紅葉散策とあわせて、芸術の秋に、日本の豊かな伝統文化と晩秋の情趣を心ゆくまで満喫してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
We now know the official cause of death for Richard Riehle . The prolific character actor, known for his work in Office Space, Bridesmaids, Casino and much more, died from a stroke, with oropharyngeal cancer, which affects the throat, listed as the underlying cause, according to his death certificate obtained by TMZ .

Riehle died October 15 at his home in Los Angeles. He was 78.

Related Stories

Richard Riehle Dies: ‘Office Space’ & ‘Bridesmaids’ Actor Was 78

2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries

“We are deeply saddened to confirm the passing of our beloved client, Richard Riehle, this past weekend,” Riehle’s reps said in a statement to Deadline.

“A remarkable actor whose career in theater, film, and television spanned nearly five decades and more than 400 projects, Richard leaves behind an extraordinary legacy,” the statement continued. “Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity. Our industry has lost an exceptional talent, and our community has lost a truly wonderful man.”

One of Riehle’s best-known roles as was a Tom Smykowski, a cynical Initech product manager, in Mike Judge’s 1999 satirical comedy Office Space , in which he appeared alongside Ron Livingston, Jennifer Aniston, Stephen Root and Gary Cole.

His additional film credits included Joyride (1977), Black Rain (1989), Of Mice and Men (1992), Free Willy (1993), The Fugitive (1993), Lightning Jack (1994), Casino (1995), Ghosts of Mississippi (1996), The Odd Couple II (1998), Lethal Weapon 4 (1998), Office Space (1999), Deuce Bigalo: Make Gigolo (1999), Joe Dirt (2001), Beethoven’s 5th (2003), Wedding Crashers (2005), National Lampoon’s Dom Daze 2 (2006), Red (2008), Halloween II (2009), Bridesmaids (2011), A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas (2011), Texas Chainsaw 3D (2013), Lovesick (2014). His last film credit was in 2026, in The Cowboy Killer .

Riehle’s television work included TV movie The Other Side of Hell , followed by My Two Dads (1989), Dragnet (1989) and Falcon Crest (1989). He also appeared on Quantum Leap , Murder, Show Wrote , L.A. Law , Ferris Bueller , The Golden Girls , Roseanne , Star Trek: The Next Generation , Ally McBeal , The Practice , Buffy the Vampire Slayer , Chicago Hope and Home Improvement , among others.

His most recent TV credits included American Housewife (2019) and Fuller House (2020). His last role was playing Warden Reynolds in HBO’s Barry (2023).
